column2: Primary-prevention ICD: LVEF ≤ 35% despite ≥ 3 months of optimal therapy, NYHA II–III and reasonable survival. Recheck EF after myocarditis or peripartum disease.
Spironolactone cut HFrEF mortality by ~30% (RALES), eplerenone in milder HF (EMPHASIS-HF). Diuretics relieve congestion but activate RAAS.
In chronic HF digoxin is given 62.5–250 µg daily without loading; levels only if toxicity, renal impairment or interactions. It reduces admissions, not mortality.
Heart-failure CXR: cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, bat-wing oedema, Kerley B lines, effusions, fissure fluid. The left lung has no horizontal fissure.
Breathless at rest with gross oedema: relieve congestion first with a loop diuretic; start/titrate ACEi and beta-blocker once less congested.
ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalaemia (less aldosterone), not hypokalaemia; also cough, angioedema, first-dose hypotension and AKI. Check U&E before and after dose changes.
An ICD is the only proven way to prevent sudden death in HCM: after aborted arrest (as here) or when the ESC 5-year risk is ≥ 6%.
Ascites, tender liver, jaundice, AF, oedema, orthopnoea and systolic JVP waves (TR) mean congestive (biventricular) failure. Cirrhosis does not raise the JVP.
Decompensated aortic stenosis first raises LA and pulmonary venous pressure, giving bibasal crackles; raised JVP and oedema follow only with right failure.
Venous hypertension causes upper-lobe diversion; 'lower-lobe diversion' is not a sign. Cardiomegaly, effusions, alveolar oedema and Kerley B lines are typical.
Nausea, anorexia and yellow vision/halos are digoxin toxicity, promoted by hypokalaemia, CKD and interacting drugs; give Digifab for life-threatening toxicity.
Acute LV failure (likely MI) raises pulmonary capillary pressure, causing hydrostatic oedema, hypoxaemia and hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis). Permeability = ARDS.
Exertional breathlessness with an S3 suggests heart failure; a raised BNP/NT-proBNP supports it and NICE then arranges echo (within 2 or 6 weeks).
A perihilar bat-wing pattern is alveolar oedema; in a breathless smoker the likeliest cause is LV failure. TR causes systemic, not pulmonary, congestion.
Syncope during exertion is a red flag (HCM, anomalous coronaries, long QT, ARVC, WPW): ECG and echo, and no competitive sport until cleared.
EF 38% after heart failure (stage C) needs prognostic therapy: ACEi (or ARB/ARNI) plus beta-blocker, then MRA and SGLT2i, even if now asymptomatic.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (EF < 45% late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum): about half recover fully; recurrence in later pregnancies is common.
HFrEF still NYHA III on ACEi, beta-blocker and diuretic: add an MRA (spironolactone) with K⁺/renal monitoring; SGLT2i and ARNI follow.
Multiply transfused patients develop iron-overload cardiomyopathy: check ferritin and transferrin saturation, then cardiac MRI T2*; chelation can reverse it.
BNP < 100 pg/mL (NT-proBNP < 300 acutely) has a high negative predictive value: acute heart failure is unlikely, so look for another cause.
BNP causes natriuresis, vasodilatation and inhibits RAAS and sympathetic activity. Sacubitril raises natriuretic peptides by blocking neprilysin.
BNP/NT-proBNP is secreted mainly by ventricular myocytes in response to stretch; ANP comes from the atria.
BNP can be raised without LV failure in COPD (RV strain), PE, AF, sepsis, CKD, cirrhosis and age > 70. Obesity and HF drugs lower it.
Pulmonary flow murmur, fixed wide S2 splitting and incomplete RBBB (RSR' in V1) with plethoric lungs is a secundum ASD.
About half of patients with coarctation have a bicuspid aortic valve; both are common in Turner syndrome.
Hypertension in a young man with an arm BP difference suggests coarctation at or near the left subclavian origin (left arm lower). Check radiofemoral delay.
Inferior rib notching (ribs 3–8) from dilated intercostal collaterals is classic of coarctation, rarely before age 8; the '3 sign' is another clue.
Significant coarctation (gradient ≥ 20 mmHg or hypertension) is repaired: stenting in suitable adults, surgery in infants. Lifelong follow-up for recoarctation.
A small secundum ASD without pulmonary hypertension is well tolerated in pregnancy (mWHO II); routine follow-up is enough.
Isolated secundum ASD has very low endocarditis risk; prophylaxis is not indicated (NICE never routinely; ESC only for high-risk lesions).
In ASD the shunt keeps RV volume high throughout respiration, so S2 is widely split with a fixed interval. Paradoxical splitting = LBBB or severe AS.
Secundum ASD typically shows RSR' in V1 (incomplete RBBB) with right axis deviation; left axis deviation suggests a primum defect.
Eisenmenger develops in a minority of large unrepaired shunts (< 10% of adult ASDs); a small secundum ASD carries low risk.
Exertional collapse with deep cyanosis in congenital heart disease is a tetralogy of Fallot spell (RVOT spasm increases right-to-left shunt).
Eisenmenger syndrome: shunt reversal causes cyanosis, clubbing and erythrocytosis; life expectancy is markedly reduced and pregnancy is very high-risk.
A small restrictive VSD gives a loud harsh pansystolic murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge despite a trivial shunt (maladie de Roger).
Clubbing and cyanosis of toes but not fingers (differential cyanosis) is PDA with pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal.
Maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies damage the fetal conduction system, causing congenital complete heart block; monitor the fetal heart from 16 weeks.
Limb ischaemia in a young woman with a childhood murmur suggests paradoxical embolism through an ASD/PFO; echo with bubble study shows the shunt.
Fixed S2 splitting with flow murmurs and a stroke in a young adult suggests paradoxical embolism across an ASD; confirm with bubble echo and consider closure.
A small VSD causes no overload or pulmonary hypertension; its main long-term risk is infective endocarditis. Many small muscular VSDs close spontaneously.
VSD gives a harsh holosystolic murmur at the mid/lower left sternal border. ASD = pulmonary flow murmur; PDA = continuous machinery murmur.
Significant PDA in a preterm infant is closed medically with a COX inhibitor (ibuprofen/indomethacin) or paracetamol; prostaglandin E1 keeps it open.
VSD complications: heart failure, Eisenmenger, aortic regurgitation, endocarditis. AF reflects atrial overload (ASD, mitral disease), not VSD.
Thyrotoxic AF: a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol) controls rate and adrenergic symptoms; antithyroid treatment restores sinus rhythm. Amiodarone worsens thyroid disease.
